How to use this page

  • It shows the form. Each draft follows the course template and is written to the rubric, so you can see what a complete section looks like.
  • It is not an answer key. Your organization, model and data are your own; copy the habits, not the content.
  • Its model gets tested. The current version is careful work, and careful work can still rest on a model that turns out to be incomplete. When the evidence calls for a revision, the revision is posted with what was learned and why.

Project Brief version 1

1. The organization

Fernhill Software is a useful fiction: a business-software firm with about 1,100 engineers in 120 product teams. It hires engineers on technical skill and promotes its strongest into management, where some struggle. In 2025, as AI coding tools arrive, an AI enthusiast on the leadership team proposes a reorganization: hire professional managers on people skill instead of promoting engineers; make each team’s engineer-manager its technical lead, keeping technical judgment but managing no one; and let AI fill the manager’s technical gaps. What Fernhill does: it adopts the plan in all 120 teams in July 2025, with AI at the same time.

2. The model

A team delivers when two jobs get done: coordinating people and resolving technical unknowns. The proposal splits those jobs between a manager and a lead, with AI assisting both.

  1. People skill lowers coordination friction: less work sits blocked on other people, more so in bigger teams.
  2. AI covers the manager’s technical gaps: it explains technical status, checks estimates, and drafts plans.
  3. Technical judgment stays with the lead, who resolves the team’s unknowns as the engineer-manager did, so nothing technical is lost.

In short: the reorganization puts people skill in the manager’s chair without losing technical judgment, so delivery rises.

For the model to be right, the professional managers must have more people skill than the engineer-managers they replace; AI must cover the manager’s technical gap on hard work as well as easy; the leads must accept their new role; and nothing else that affects delivery may change at the same time. What stays unmeasured: whether AI actually covers the manager’s gap; licenses show only access.

3. The question

Should Fernhill replace engineer-managers with professional managers backed by technical leads and AI? The rollout answers with one comparison: before and after July 2025 across all 120 teams, which shows the whole package as adopted, if nothing else changed.

4. The prediction

Stated before looking at this version’s data:

  • Delivery rises after July 2025, by about 5 percentage points, after a dip in the first quarter.
  • People-skill ratings rise after the reorganization.
  • The rise holds on hard quarters as well as easy ones, because AI covers the technical gap.

The model is wrong if any of these holds:

  • Delivery is no higher after the reorganization than before.
  • People-skill ratings rise but delivery doesn’t. Then people skill isn’t what drives delivery.
  • Delivery rises on easy quarters but falls on hard ones. Then AI doesn’t cover the technical gap.

5. The data sketch

The data. Fernhill’s records, one row per team per quarter, July 2023 to June 2026 (1,440 rows); simulated, since Fernhill is fictional. The variables, by concept: the change (before or after July 2025; manager type; AI licenses); the manager (people-skill rating on the eight Project Oxygen behaviors; hours work sits blocked on other teams); the work (difficulty rated at quarter’s close); and the outcome (share of committed milestones delivered on time).

6. The disciplinary anchor

Whom to promote (organizational management). Firms promote their best performers, who then make worse managers (Peter and Hull, 1969; Benson, Li and Shue, 2019). People skill keeps teams together, and Google’s Project Oxygen ranked technical skill last of eight manager behaviors (Hoffman and Tadelis, 2021; Garvin, 2013).

The work itself (operations management). Cheaper knowledge means fewer problems go up the hierarchy, and AI helps less experienced workers most (Garicano, 2000; Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, 2025).

The method. A before-and-after comparison of the whole firm, with eight quarters of history as the baseline.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) to turn the leadership proposal into relationships and match each concept to a record. It suggested checking for other 2025 changes that could move delivery; I listed that as an assumption, since the customer migration is a workload change, not a management change. It suggested rating difficulty at planning; I rejected that, since the quarter-close review already rates every quarter.

Data & Methods draft version 1

1. Unit of observation

One row of my data is one product team in one quarter, because the reorganization happens team by team and delivery is counted by the quarter. There are 1,440 rows: 120 teams over 12 quarters, July 2023 to June 2026, eight before the reorganization and four after. Each team has one manager at a time, so a row is also one manager’s quarter, which is what my model is about.

2. Variable table

Concept Variable Kind Source What it misses
Reorganization manager_type Labels HR system Mid-quarter changes
Before or after period Labels Calendar Half-done quarters
People skill people_rating Measurement (share) Upward survey Likability; non-response
AI ai_access Yes/No IT licenses Actual use
Difficulty hard_close Yes/No Close review Difficulty seen beforehand
Delivery delivered_share Measurement (share) Planning tool Customer value; renegotiation

3. Data source

Fernhill’s HR system, quarterly upward feedback survey, IT licenses, quarter-close review, and planning tool, read through People Analytics, cover all 120 teams for all 12 quarters. The file also holds records my model doesn’t call for (team size, escalations, waits, departures); Gemini suggested describing them, and I left them out. Fernhill is a useful fiction, so these records are simulated, but not from the model above: they come from a model this version doesn’t see, whose units are these team-quarters and whose relationships, noise, and assumptions are published in Module 3. Until then, I treat them as the firm’s records.

4. Quality concern

The people-skill rating is the most likely to mislead. It is missing for 102 of 1,440 team-quarters (7%), and may be mismeasured: favorable answers can reward a likable manager, and a manager new in July 2025 is rated after one quarter. If so, I would see blanks bunched in some teams or quarters, and new managers’ ratings jumping in their first quarters. I will report the blanks and never fill them in, compare each team with itself before and after, and read the rating as the team’s view, not a measure of skill.

5. First description

Delivery (delivered_share). Kind: a measurement, a share from 0 to 1. How many: 1,440, none blank. Middle: median 0.69; mean 0.65, pulled down by a tail of bad quarters. Spread: half fall between 0.50 and 0.83; the range is 0 to 1. Shape: skewed left, with a long tail of quarters that delivered little (30 under 5%). Choice: each team-quarter counts once, whatever its size; weighting by milestones gives 0.64.

Against my model: not yet able to say; one variable can’t show whether delivery rose after July 2025.

People skill (people_rating). Kind: a measurement, a share of favorable answers. How many: 1,338; 102 blank (7%), as many before July 2025 as after. Middle: median 0.74, mean 0.72. Spread: half fall between 0.65 and 0.81; the range is 0.31 to 0.94. Shape: skewed left: a few teams rate their manager far below the rest. Choice: blanks left out, not filled in.

Against my model: not yet able to say; the model needs ratings to be higher under professional managers, and one variable can’t show that.

Difficulty (hard_close). Kind: Yes/No. How many: 1,440, none blank. Middle, spread and shape: 0.43 rated hard (619 quarters); with two values, the proportion says it all. Against my model: not yet able to say, but there are enough quarters of each kind to test whether a gain holds on hard quarters.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for the counts, middles, spreads, and histograms. I added a milestone-weighted figure to its average, and rejected its offer to fill blank ratings, since a filled-in rating is a measurement nobody took.

The data version 1

Download fernhill_v1.csv 1,440 rows × 19 columns: one row per team per quarter, July 2023 to June 2026.

Fernhill is a useful fiction, so these records are simulated. Every number in the drafts above comes from this file; check any of them with Gemini.

What each column records
ColumnKindWhat it records
team_idLabelsThe team, T001 to T120
quarterDates and times2023Q3 to 2026Q2
periodLabelspre = July 2023 to June 2025; pilot = Fernhill's planning label for July 2025 onward
ai_accessYes/NoAI tools licensed to the team
team_sizeCountsEngineers on the team
manager_typeLabelsengineer (an engineer promoted to manager) or professional (a manager hired on people skill)
tech_scoreMeasurementThe manager's technical assessment at hire, 0 to 100 (a coding test for engineers; a literacy test for professional managers)
people_ratingMeasurement (a share)Share of favorable answers about the manager on the eight Project Oxygen behaviors, from the team's upward feedback survey; blank if the team didn't answer
lead_former_managerYes/NoWhether the team's technical lead used to be its manager; blank where there is no lead
hard_closeYes/NoWork rated hard at the quarter-close review, after it ended
escalationsCountsTechnical questions the team sent up for a decision
esc_open_at_closeCountsEscalations still unanswered at the quarter's close
esc_wait_hrsMeasurementTypical hours an escalation waited for an answer; a few blank
blocked_hoursMeasurementTypical hours a ticket sat blocked on another team

milestones_deliveredCountsOf those, milestones delivered by their dates
delivered_shareMeasurement (a share)Delivered ÷ committed: the outcome
